profiles.name: Law, Society & Justice
profiles.actualContent: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
profiles.judgment: introduces legal, social and normative perspectives on law and justice for examining religion in public life Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
profiles.actualContent: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about the ways we think and act—about, amongst other things, the nature of knowledge, consciousness, our responsibilities towards others, freedom, the existence of god, whether and in what sense our lives can be said to have meaning. Philosophical questions might appear to be simple at first glance, and many of us would have immediate intuitive responses to at least some of them. But providing coherent, lucid, and compelling responses to philosophical questions is a very challenging endeavor. This course introduces central themes from the Western philosophical tradition, spanning 2,500 years of history from the ancient Greeks to cutting-edge work from our own time. We will become familiar with the issues discussed by philosophers, inquire into their significance and their relation to thought in other disciplines, such as psychology, law, physics, computer science, and political science. And, even more importantly, we will acquaint ourselves with theoretical methods and tools that have been used by philosophers to support their conclusions and ideas. 3 Through detailed engagement with central philosophical ideas and arguments, we will develop a critical perspective and approach the rewarding task of articulating our own views on philosophical issues. We shall see that philosophy is a paradigmatic exercise in critical reasoning: it provides an opportunity to develop reasoning skills through rigorous and precise argumentation concerning issues of great importance to our lives.
profiles.judgment: Broad2500yearWestern philosophical questions includingGod/meaning: genuine philosophical contribution without systematicChristian theology.

profiles.name: World Myth & Literature
profiles.actualContent: How do ancient literary myths compare to the literature of other parts of the world? What can these parallels tell us about age-old global connections, or even about universal human themes? This course explores what might be tentatively named the literary silk road, but also taps into the narrative traditions of continents beyond. For instance, we investigate the similarities between the stories of ancient epic poems, from Homer to Virgil, with the Indian epic Mahabharata; we look at the strands between the romance novels of the classical world and those from Byzantine and Arabic literature. We explore how storytelling is expressed beyond text, for instance in oral traditions, visual culture, or in theatrical performance. The tradition of depicting mythical narratives is common to cultures all over the world. What are the processes of transmitting text into image? How do these literary images differ across cultures? Spanning four millennia and at least three continents, this course will examine how literary stories of myth form a deep cultural foundation, and how they deal with universal human themes like love, loyalty, power, and friendship.
profiles.judgment: Comparative literary myths/Mahabharata/epic and narrative transmission: real religious-cultural narrative, not scriptural exegesis or theological method.

profiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
profiles.actualContent: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
profiles.judgment: introduces sociological theories of institutions, inequality and collective life for analysing religious change and identity Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
profiles.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
profiles.judgment: General academic/personal formation. Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
profiles.actualContent: How does making things define human existence and societies, from their earliest beginnings to the end of antiquity and beyond? This course examines this question first, through the pragmatics of manufacture in relation to religious, social, and gendered identities, from Çatalhöyük (Türkiye) in 10.000 BCE and the region of Kush (Sudan) around 8.000 BCE, to classical Athens and Rome, and from the Harappan Valley to the Philippines. In every context we will explore the artefacts, their production and their makers. By exploring these, we can discover the story of the communities that made them. We will look at individual manufacturing techniques from settlements in different parts of the world, and how the objects made in (urban) communities could help people negotiate identity. We will look at the social and environmental impact of these crafts, and how technologies have helped shape social identity through the ancient world. The course has an experimental component where we design an educational activity surrounding an archaeological or ancient craft-related theme, for which a main requirement is that it involves a hands-on activity. Finally, we will explore how archaeological research methods can be used in contemporary settings.
profiles.judgment: Material production and religious/social/gender identities with archaeology/craft: real religious material culture, not liturgy/pastoral theology.

profiles.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
profiles.actualContent: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
profiles.judgment: teaches qualitative design, interpretation and reflexivity for investigating lived meanings and communities Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Social Psychology
profiles.actualContent: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
profiles.judgment: examines social influence, group processes, attitudes and belief formation Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
profiles.actualContent: This course offers a broad approach to human rights: the legal, the historical and the theoretical/philosophical. In the first part of the course, human rights will mainly be studied in a legal way, adopting a legal perspective. Students will be introduced to the catalogue of human rights as positive law. Human rights treaties, the monitoring mechanisms and case law on human rights will be explored. This knowledge will be tested in a mid-term exam (multiple choice). In the second part, students will delve into a more historical and philosophical understanding of human rights. We will investigate the rise of the language of human rights in the 17th and 18th century, its culmination in the US Bill of Rights (1791) and the Déclaration des Droits de l’Homme et du Citoyen (1789). We will explore the further developments of the language in the 20th century in particular, which brought a great extension of the number and application of human rights. Students will read landmark cases that touch upon contentious, and often politicised disputes between liberty and equality. Some emphasis in this course will be given to natural law and its connection to human rights. We will delve into the classical and medieval scholarship on natural law, starting with Plato’s and Aquinas’ views on right and wrong. This will be compared to the modern views on the same going back to Hobbes and Locke, the latter considered to be the founding father of the rights paradigm. Human rights in today’s traditional societies will be investigated through selected case studies.
profiles.judgment: studies human-rights law and philosophical foundations relevant to freedom, equality and religion Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
profiles.actualContent: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science.
profiles.judgment: provides concepts of authority, liberty, justice and political obligation for analysing religion and politics Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
profiles.actualContent: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
profiles.judgment: compares political institutions and state-society relations that shape religion in public life Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
profiles.actualContent: This course examines key debates on modern art through a carefully selected range of themes and topics. A central focus is the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions. By exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies, students will gain insight into how art institutions shape public perception and understanding of modern and contemporary art.
profiles.judgment: analyses how museums and curatorial strategies shape public interpretations of art and heritage Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
profiles.actualContent: In this course on constitutional law and administrative law, students will undertake an exploration of the essential principles of these foundational legal fields. A comparative approach is used, examining and analyzing the constitutional law of five different legal systems. A constitution is the “fundamental and organic law of a nation or state that establishes the institutions and apparatus of government, defines the scope of governmental sovereign powers, and guarantees individual civil rights and civil liberties”, and ther efore, constitutional law is the “field of law dealing with aspects of constitutional provisions, such as restrictions on government powers and guarantees of rights.” (Blacks Law Dictionary 8 Ed, Garner et al eds, West 2004.) Yet, constitutional law is so much more than is suggested by these definitions. At the center of the modern constitutional state is the law, which protects peace, freedom and security. It is this law that is controlling, not the human actors in a state. In order that all may have acce ss to and rely on it, this law should be enshrined in a written document. Democracy demands a law that is enacted by a legislative body after public debate about its contents. The foundational values of a legal culture are written down in its constitution. The constitution takes up established values, tried and tested institutions and reliable political experience and passes them on to the next generation in a binding manner.
profiles.judgment: compares constitutional systems, fundamental rights and religious constitutions, directly supporting religion-state analysis Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Ethics
profiles.actualContent: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.
profiles.judgment: develops ethical reasoning for questions of justice, equality, environment and contested values Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: African Art & Heritage
profiles.actualContent: This course offers an introduction to African art and heritage, with a special focus on the rich artistic traditions of western Africa. Students will study the region’s diverse visual languages, uncovering how sculptures, masks, and other forms of visual expression embody cultural, religious, and social meaning. The course also traces Africa’s enduring influence on global art, from the appropriations of European artists like Picasso and Matisse to modern and contemporary African and African diaspora artists who reinterpret traditional forms in often unexpected ways. A significant component of the course addresses ethical and institutional questions surrounding the collection and display of African art. Through case studies and critical debate, students will explore the legacy of colonial-era looting, the politics of museum acquisitions, and the growing movement for repatriation of African art to their place of origin. Designed for students interested in art history, cultural heritage, and museum studies, the course encourages you to see African art not just as objects, but as living stories: resilient, resonant, and still unfolding.
profiles.judgment: WestAfrican art with religious/social meaning and colonial collection/repatriation: real partial religious heritage, not Christian doctrine/history.

profiles.name: Philosophy of Mind
profiles.actualContent: o What is the nature of consciousness? o What explains the identity of selves over time? How have different philosophical traditions thought about this issue? o Can the mind be explained in neurobiological terms? o Are large language models conscious? Can they ever be? o What can we learn from dream states about conscious experience? o What can perceptual illusions teach us about our awareness of the world? o What are the differences between human and animal consciousness? These are some of the questions explored in the philosophy of mind, an important field of philosophy since early modernity. The field has come to prominence and maturation in the past decades alongside advances in the scientific study of the human mind, research on animal minds, and innovations in computing. In this course, we will focus both on important work from the history of the field and on contributions from recent scholarship. We shall begin with exploration of the nature of selves and personal identity, looking at historical sources in the Western tradition, contemporary debate, as well as the theory of the self in Buddhist thought. Detailed discussion of approaches to the mind-body problem, a key issue in the philosophy of mind, will follow. Additional topics to be examined in the course include: the possibility of intelligent and conscious machines, animal minds, dream states, the significance of transformative experiences, and the impact of novel technologies on the ways we experience the world.
profiles.judgment: Mind/self/consciousness includingBuddhistself: genuine comparative philosophical idea, not Christian theological anthropology.

profiles.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
profiles.actualContent: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
profiles.judgment: conducts applied research on resilience to radicalisation and develops evidence-based materials Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
profiles.actualContent: In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_ Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_ This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
profiles.judgment: AncientAthenian democracy intertwined with myth/religion, artefacts andassemblysimulation: genuine partial contribution, not churchhistory orcanonlaw.

profiles.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
profiles.actualContent: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
profiles.judgment: Actualcontent assumes introductory andModernSociology despiteformalNONE; primary route lacksModernSociology. Civil society theory/CSO field enquiry is not religious-community ethnography by default.

profiles.name: Media & Race
profiles.actualContent: Whose stories are remembered and whose are erased? What do the stories un/told teach us about power, privilege, and resistance? How do cultural expressions and forms like film, photographs, and music address systemic racism, critique the present, and envision just futures? These questions steer this course. Addressing them reveals links between past and present that students explore in final podcasts grounded in research and fueled by passion. Race, at the heart of American history and life, is at the center of this class. We begin in the late 19th century with the “end” of slavery and continue into the 21st century with the advent of ICE. Throughout the term we explore the ways media supports systems of oppression and empowers the oppressed.
profiles.judgment: studies storytelling, race, power and systemic exclusion through critical media analysis and production Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
profiles.actualContent: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.
profiles.judgment: RenaissanceItalian art and Islamic-court/globalMediterranean exchange: religious-cultural context, not a theology course.

profiles.name: Writing Art's Histories
profiles.actualContent: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
profiles.judgment: develops visual analysis and art-historical writing for interpreting identity, belief and heritage Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Great Literary Works
profiles.actualContent: This course is based on a selection of major literary texts which should be considered essential for every LAS student’s cultural capital: texts that for centuries have inspired Western culture, visual arts and theatre, and which resonate themes that preoccupy social sciences and philosophy. The course is a chronological overview of literature ranging from the earliest monuments (the epic of Gilgamesh) to post-modernity. Within this framework students will read primary (literary) and secondary (critical, theoretical) texts debating what it means to be human, mortal, female, male, or child, or what it means to be responsible, free, a member of family or other community, to be civilized or barbarian. What makes literature different from anecdote? Why are some children’s texts indebted to philosophical tale? Probing these and many other questions, students will be invited to analyse literary representations of home, labour, leisure, duty, love, leadership, organized religion, and memory, and try to correlate these topics with various artistic forms used by writers. In this way the course is an encounter with diverse genres: heroic epic, philosophical tale, fairy tale, short story, autobiography, essay and novella. With this broad approach to themes and forms in the Western literary heritage, the course is an alternative introduction to literary studies, and of fundamental value to everyone interested in literary and cultural studies.
profiles.judgment: analyses literary representations of organised religion, duty, memory and community across historical periods Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Peace & Conflict
profiles.actualContent: Peace and Conflict Studies is an interdisciplinary field that explores the causes, consequences, and potential solutions to both violent and nonviolent conflicts. Its goal is to understand the complex factors that contribute to conflict, the dynamics of violence, and the strategies for achieving lasting peace. The field encompasses insights from history, sociology, political science, international relations, and law, among other disciplines . This course introduces the field by examining and assessing multi ple theories of conflict and peacebuilding in the context of ongoing and past conflicts at regional, national and international levels. Peace and Conflict Studies is not only interdisciplinary but also shaped by diverse analytical perspectives. Some approaches emphasize structural inequality , clashing ideologies, and others focus on humiliation, historical wounds, and identity -based grievances, particularly in colonial or postcolonial contexts. Each lens draws attention to different forms of evidence and different peacebuilding strategies. As a result, this course demonstrates the importance of adopting a holistic approach that includes in ternational, institutional, and state -led elements, as well as cultural, interpersonal, and bottom-up actions led by civil society. The course uses “Travelling Concepts” as a tool for critically applying an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will compare how “justice,” “truth,” or “reconciliation” are mobilized in legal vs.
profiles.judgment: studies ideological conflict, radicalisation, violence, reconciliation and peacebuilding Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Sustainability Essentials I
profiles.actualContent: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3
profiles.judgment: Actual environmental science, technology, sustainability or governance: Sustainability Essentials I. Relevant to environmental responsibility; no evidence of theological or religious-ecology method. establishes the core sustainability concepts and systems vocabulary that the environmental-ethics concept evaluates

profiles.name: Climate Change
profiles.actualContent: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
profiles.judgment: Actual environmental science, technology, sustainability or governance: Climate Change. Relevant to environmental responsibility; no evidence of theological or religious-ecology method. provides the climate science whose consequences the moral argument is about

profiles.name: Sustainability Essentials II
profiles.actualContent: ENSGATE201 - Sustainability Essentials II serves as the Gateway course to several 300 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy these course in the cluster. We will focus on three main topics (Waves, Chemistry and Material science) and on how they relate to Sustainability. You will have the opportunity to explore the topics in individual reflective journals as well as a project at the end of the course. In the project, you will use what you learned to analyse and discuss green washing. 3
profiles.judgment: Actual environmental science, technology, sustainability or governance: Sustainability Essentials II. Relevant to environmental responsibility; no evidence of theological or religious-ecology method. extends sustainability analysis to systems, transitions and assessment methods

profiles.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
profiles.actualContent: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
profiles.judgment: studies environmental justice movements and collective action on ecological harm Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
profiles.actualContent: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
profiles.judgment: analyses contested climate communication across texts, film, exhibitions, protest art and social media Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
profiles.actualContent: To prepare our society for a circular and sustainable future, we need to evaluate the environmental impact of products, processes, or services throughout their entire lifecycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal, or ideally re-usage as new raw materials. To do this, we have to understand the environmental, social and health consequences of products and processes and develop a strategic planning for future activi- ties. ENSSUST112 - Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economywill be heavily focussed on “learning by doing”, rather than by just studying books. Therefore most of this course will consist of analysing different products, processes and services and include guest lectures by experts working in the field of sustainability and circularity. 3

profiles.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
profiles.actualContent: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. profiles.name: Philosophy of Emotion
profiles.actualContent: Emotions are a basic aspect of human experience, but they have been, throughout the history of philosophy, contrasted with and sidelined by the pursuit of rationality. They seem to be of important value, central to our well-being, and yet they can often be deeply messy and puzzling. This course provides the opportunity to engage with key questions in the study of emotions from a philosophical perspective. The core topics we shall explore in the course are: (i) The nature of emotions. What are emotions? Are they like beliefs, feelings, or perceptions? (ii) Emotions and ethics. What is the role of emotion in well-being? How important are emotions for moral judgment? In what ways are emotions significant for moral motivation and character? (iii) Emotions and rationality. What does it mean for an emotion to be appropriate? What makes emotions rational or irrational? (iv) Particular emotions: love, fear, disgust; emotions and moods. (v) Emotions and politics. What is the place of the emotions in the context of political projects? Are there emotions we should cultivate as a political community, others we should reject? (vi) Emotions and art. Are we able to experience genuine emotion towards works of fiction? Are there emotions that are specific to the appreciation of art? What is the relation between aesthetic emotions and moral emotions? GOSPHIL311: Philosophy of Emotion We will consider sources from the history of philosophy as well contemporary research on the emotions from philosophy and additional disciplines.
profiles.judgment: examines emotion, rationality and human experience as dimensions of belief and public persuasion Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.

profiles.name: Calling Bullshit
profiles.actualContent: The world is rife with misinformation. To function properly in any field, it is important that you are able to recognize it adequately handle it. In this course, you will develop your “bullshit-detector”. The course is structured around the following four questions: What is bullshit? The word “bullshit” is subject to a lot of philosophical essays, of which you will read some. It is important to get a clear view of what we mean by it, and what distinguishes it from lying, fake news, mis/disinformation, nonsense or baloney, false beliefs, or the slightly different “horseshit”. We will discuss this extensively in the first sessions. We will then proceed with a historical overview of misinformation and the role it played in politics and society as a whole. It is -kind of- reassuring that bullshit is nothing new: Fake news and smear campaigns can be traced back to Sumerian clay tablets and were prominent in Roman society (ask Mark Anthony!). Understanding the historical context enables us to recognize patterns. What makes us vulnerable to bullshit? We will discuss common biases in human thinking and social pressures that make us vulnerable to bullshit and other types of misinformation. We are all human, so everybody can fall victim to false beliefs. Understanding our own way of thinking and the way our social environment influences us, helps us to process information more reliably and sharpens our critical thinking skills. How can you recognize bullshit? You will learn how to detect and distinguish several types of bullshit using a taxonomy of bullshit.
profiles.judgment: Actual environmental science, technology, sustainability or governance: Calling Bullshit. Relevant to environmental responsibility; no evidence of theological or religious-ecology method. examines misinformation, cognitive bias, pseudoscience and credibility in public knowledge claims

profiles.name: Governance of Sustainability
profiles.actualContent: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.
profiles.judgment: Actual environmental science, technology, sustainability or governance: Governance of Sustainability. Relevant to environmental responsibility; no evidence of theological or religious-ecology method. analyses how sustainability is governed, regulated and contested across institutions

profiles.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
profiles.actualContent: Ecology is the scientific study of the distribution and abundance of organisms and the interactions that determine distribution and abundance. Over the past decades, ecology has grown from an obscure science into a position at the forefront of public and political consciousness. Applied ecology has become an important scientific tool to address important political and environmental issues. Ecology is generally divided into 3 levels: the individual organism, the population (consisting of individuals of the same species) and the community, in which several species are living together. In addition, ecology focuses on the relationship between living creatures and their chemical and physical surroundings, which together make up an ecosystem. Ecology is a complex science. It draws on many areas of knowledge such as organic and inorganic chemistry, plant and animal biology, physiology, meteorology, and even economics. This course focuses on the basic principles of ecology, from individuals to ecosystems. We then proceed to environmental conditions and resources, and the 4 levels of ecology: individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems. Two weeks will be spent on ecological modelling, as an important tool for understanding and predicting ecological systems. We will conclude with some actual cases of applied ecology.
profiles.judgment: Actual environmental science, technology, sustainability or governance: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works. Relevant to environmental responsibility; no evidence of theological or religious-ecology method. explains how ecosystems function, which the value claims made about nature presuppose

profiles.name: Media & the Environment
profiles.actualContent: Media and the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media. You study how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt, and acted upon. The course introduces key concepts such as the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested ideas of nature, and indigenous and postcolonial media. You use these concepts as analytical tools to examine how environmental meaning is produced across different media forms and cultural contexts. The main goal of the course is to help you analyze environmental media critically and precisely. You learn how film, photography, sound, and digital media make ecological processes, environmental risk, and human and nonhuman relations visible and intelligible. The course emphasizes close analysis of images, narratives, and aesthetic strategies, as well as comparison across media genres and historical moments. You also examine how media translate scientific knowledge and lived experience into stories, images, and affects that shape public understanding, sustainability discourse, and political judgment. Questions of agency, scale, temporality, and responsibility guide your analysis throughout the course. The course combines sustained reading with structured discussion and applied analytical work. You work with scholarly texts, media examples, and guided exercises, and you complete either a final analytical paper or a media-based project. This combination reflects the core idea of the course.
profiles.judgment: examines how media frame contested environmental meanings and mobilise public responses Actual content supports its own discipline; no warranted biblical-language/exegesis, doctrine, liturgy or pastoral/theological-method equivalence.
